@dataclass
class Instance:
    # One problem instance plus the extra values computed in Section 0
    name: str
    n: int                     # number of candidate models
    m: int                     # number of resources
    p: np.ndarray              # utility of each model, shape (n,)
    R: np.ndarray              # resource use: R[i, j] = amount of resource i used by model j, shape (m, n)
    b: np.ndarray              # capacity of each resource, shape (m,)
    optimum: float = None      # true best utility (exact solver, §0.1) - used ONLY for scoring
    bound: float = None        # Lagrangian upper bound (own code, §0.2) - for information
    duals: np.ndarray = None   # shadow price of each resource (own code, §0.2) - used by the repair

def load(path, name):
    # Load a file with the provided helper and sanity-check its contents
    n, m, p, R, b = load_workload_instance(path)
    assert p.shape == (n,) and R.shape == (m, n) and b.shape == (m,)     # shapes match n and m
    assert (R >= 0).all() and (p > 0).all()                              # no negative values
    assert (R <= b[:, None]).all(), "every single model fits on its own"
    return Instance(name, n, m, p, R, b)

def find_data_file(*names, folders=(".", "data")):
    # Look for the file next to this notebook or in ./data, under any of the given names
    # (Canvas downloads sometimes add " (1)" to the file name)
    for folder in folders:
        for name in names:
            path = Path(folder) / name
            if path.exists():
                return str(path)
    raise FileNotFoundError(f"Cannot find {names[0]}. Place it in the same folder as this notebook.")

On Instance 2, resource 2 can only cover a third of the total demand (0.33), while resources 4 and 5 could cover almost all of it (0.95, 0.91). 0.1 Reference optimum (answer key for scoring)¶

The instances are small enough for an exact solver (mixed-integer programming via scipy.optimize.milp) to find the true best selection. It is used only to score results: the optimality gap, $100\,(f^*-f)/f^*$ (how far a run falls short of the best, in %), and the success rate (how many runs reach it).

In [3]:
def solve_reference(I):
    # Exact optimum via mixed-integer programming. Used ONLY to score the algorithms afterwards.
    # milp minimises, so we pass -p to maximise utility; integrality=1 forces every x_j to be 0 or 1.
    res = milp(-I.p, constraints=LinearConstraint(I.R, -np.inf, I.b),
               integrality=np.ones(I.n), bounds=Bounds(0, 1))
    x_opt = np.round(res.x).astype(int)
    assert (I.R @ x_opt <= I.b).all()              # double-check the answer respects every limit
    I.optimum = float(I.p @ x_opt)                 # compute the value from the 0/1 vector (avoids float noise)
    return x_opt

for I in (I1, I2):
    x_opt = solve_reference(I)
    print(f"{I.name}: optimum f* = {I.optimum:,.0f}  ({x_opt.sum()} models)\n"
          f"   resource use at optimum = {(I.R @ x_opt).astype(int)}  vs b = {I.b.astype(int)}")

0.2 Shadow prices (computed from scratch)¶

When a selection is over a limit, the repair operator (§1.1) has to decide which models to remove first. For that it needs to know how scarce each resource is. We measure this with one shadow price λᵢ ≥ 0 per resource, computed by our own Lagrangian relaxation with subgradient descent (Fisher, 1981; Held, Wolfe & Crowder, 1974):

  1. Instead of treating each capacity as a hard limit, each resource is given a price per unit used. With fixed prices the best choice is simple: take every model whose utility is higher than the price of the resources it uses.
  2. If that choice over-uses a resource, its price goes up. If it leaves capacity spare, its price goes down (never below 0).
  3. Repeat until the prices settle.

A scarce resource ends up with a positive price, and a resource with spare capacity ends up with price 0. Ranking items by such prices follows Pirkul (1987) and Chu & Beasley (1998). Only these m numbers are passed to the repair operator, never a solution. §1.4 checks them against SciPy's LP solver.

Compliance note. SciPy (permitted by the brief) is used only for the answer key (§0.1) and, in §1.4, to check our shadow-price routine. The search logic, variation operators, repair functions and the shadow-price computation are all implemented from scratch in this notebook, and no metaheuristic framework is used.

In [4]:
def greedy_lower_bound(I):
    # A quick valid selection, needed for the step-size rule below:
    # add models in order of utility per (capacity-scaled) resource use, skipping any that do not fit
    x, load = np.zeros(I.n), np.zeros(I.m)
    for j in np.argsort(-I.p / (I.R / I.b[:, None]).sum(0)):
        if (load + I.R[:, j] <= I.b).all():
            x[j] = 1
            load += I.R[:, j]
    return float(I.p @ x)

def compute_shadow_prices(I, iters=5_000, alpha=2.0, patience=50):
    # Lagrangian relaxation of the capacity limits, minimised by subgradient descent (see text above)
    lam, LB = np.zeros(I.m), greedy_lower_bound(I)    # start with every resource free (price 0)
    best_val, best_lam, stall = np.inf, lam.copy(), 0
    for _ in range(iters):
        reduced = I.p - lam @ I.R                        # each model's utility minus the price of its resources
        x = (reduced > 0).astype(float)                  # with these prices: take every model that "pays for itself"
        val = lam @ I.b + np.maximum(reduced, 0).sum()   # upper bound on the best utility for these prices
        if val < best_val - 1e-9:                        # remember the prices that gave the tightest bound
            best_val, best_lam, stall = val, lam.copy(), 0
        else:                                            # no improvement for `patience` steps -> smaller steps
            stall += 1
            if stall >= patience:
                alpha, stall = alpha / 2, 0
        g = I.b - I.R @ x                                # spare capacity (+) or overuse (-) of each resource
        if not g.any():                                  # selection uses exactly the capacity: optimal prices
            break
        # overused resource (g < 0) -> price goes up; spare resource (g > 0) -> price goes down, never below 0.
        # Step size: standard Polyak rule, (bound - LB) / |g|^2, scaled by alpha
        lam = np.maximum(0.0, lam - alpha * (val - LB) / (g @ g) * g)
    I.duals, I.bound = best_lam, best_val
    return best_lam, best_val

for I in (I1, I2):
    lam, bound = compute_shadow_prices(I)
    print(f"{I.name}: shadow prices = {np.round(lam, 3)}   "
          f"Lagrangian upper bound = {bound:,.1f}  (true optimum {I.optimum:,.0f})")

Instance 1 (n=28, m=2): shadow prices = [  4.4  107.28]   Lagrangian upper bound = 131,637.5  (true optimum 130,883)
Instance 2 (n=90, m=5): shadow prices = [0.    2.769 0.    0.    0.   ]   Lagrangian upper bound = 11,194.7  (true optimum 11,191)

Observation that shapes the design. On Instance 2 only resource 2 has a non-zero shadow price, and it is the only resource used to 100 % at the optimum (1100/1100). The other four have 15–40 % spare. So the problem behaves almost like a single-resource knapsack on resource 2, and the repair should rank models mainly by how much of resource 2 they use. On Instance 1 both resources are nearly full at the optimum (495/500 and 499/500), so both have positive prices.

1. Shared solver library¶

All algorithms are built from the same small set of interchangeable parts, so each experiment differs only in the part being tested:

Component What it does
Evaluator the only way to score a selection. It stops at the evaluation budget, counts how many candidates were valid, and records the best valid utility after every evaluation (used for the convergence curves)
ConstraintHandler classes decide how invalid selections are treated: initial() builds a starting selection, prepare() runs before scoring (e.g. repair), fitness() is the score the search compares
operators how selections change: flip and swap moves (hill climber), tournament selection, uniform crossover, bit-flip mutation (GA)
hill_climber, steady_state_ga the two search algorithms. Both work with any constraint handler
run_many, compare 30 seeded runs per variant, summary tables, Mann–Whitney U test, A12 effect size, Holm correction
In [5]:
class Evaluator:
    # Scores selections and enforces the budget. One call to evaluate() = one fitness evaluation.
    def __init__(self, inst, budget):
        self.I, self.budget, self.used, self.n_feasible = inst, int(budget), 0, 0
        self.best_util, self.best_x = 0.0, None          # best VALID selection seen so far
        self.trace = np.zeros(self.budget)               # best valid utility after each evaluation (convergence curve)

    @property
    def remaining(self):
        return self.budget - self.used

    def evaluate(self, x):
        assert self.used < self.budget, "evaluation budget exceeded"   # no algorithm can cheat the budget
        util = float(self.I.p @ x)                                     # total utility of the selection
        violation = float(np.maximum(self.I.R @ x - self.I.b, 0).sum())  # total amount over the limits (0 = valid)
        if violation == 0:
            self.n_feasible += 1
            if util > self.best_util:                                  # new best valid selection
                self.best_util, self.best_x = util, x.copy()
        self.trace[self.used] = self.best_util
        self.used += 1
        return util, violation

    def result(self):
        # Summary of one run, scored against the answer key
        if self.used < self.budget:                      # if the algorithm stopped early, carry the best value forward
            self.trace[self.used:] = self.best_util
        opt = self.I.optimum
        hit = np.flatnonzero(self.trace >= opt)          # evaluations at which the optimum had been found
        return {"best_utility": self.best_util,
                "gap_%": 100 * (opt - self.best_util) / opt,
                "hit_optimum": self.best_util >= opt,
                "evals_to_opt": hit[0] + 1 if hit.size else np.nan,   # first evaluation that reached the optimum
                "feasible_rate": self.n_feasible / max(self.used, 1),
                "evals_used": self.used}

1.1 Constraint-handling strategies¶

Three standard ways of dealing with selections that go over a limit (Coello Coello, 2002). Part 1 compares all three, and Part 3 compares the static penalty with repair.

  • Death penalty: an over-limit selection gets fitness −∞ and is never accepted. The search starts from a random valid selection, made by removing random models until everything fits.

  • Static penalty: $F(x)=f(x)-\lambda\sum_i\max(0,\;R_i x-b_i)$, i.e. utility minus a fine proportional to the total amount over the limits. The fine per unit is $\lambda=\max_{i,j:\,r_{ij}>0} p_j/r_{ij}$, the highest utility any model earns per unit of any resource, so breaking a limit never pays off (Olsen, 1994). Over-limit selections stay in the search and can act as stepping stones.

  • Greedy repair (Chu & Beasley, 1998): each model gets a value-for-money ratio $u_j = p_j / \sum_i w_i r_{ij}$ (its utility divided by a weighted sum of the resources it uses). The repair then works in two steps:

    • DROP: while the selection is over a limit, remove selected models, lowest ratio first.
    • ADD: then add unselected models, highest ratio first, whenever they fit.

    The result is always valid and full (no further model fits), and it replaces the original selection. The weights w are the shadow prices from §0.2. A simpler alternative, w = 1/b (each resource counted as a fraction of its capacity), is compared in §4.1.

    Move-preserving version: prepare(x, keep, ban) never removes the model a move has just added (keep) and never re-adds the one it has just removed (ban). Without this, the repair often undoes the move and the hill climber wastes evaluations on unchanged selections.

In [ ]:
class ConstraintHandler:
    # Base class: random starting selection, no repair. Subclasses define the fitness score.
    name = "base"
    def __init__(self, inst): self.I = inst
    def initial(self, rng):  return (rng.random(self.I.n) < 0.5).astype(np.int8)   # each model in with prob. 0.5
    def prepare(self, x, keep=-1, ban=-1): return x                                 # default: no change
    def fitness(self, util, violation): raise NotImplementedError

class DeathPenalty(ConstraintHandler):
    name = "Death penalty"
    def initial(self, rng):
        x = super().initial(rng)
        while (self.I.R @ x > self.I.b).any():                 # remove random models until everything fits
            x[rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(x))] = 0
        return x
    def fitness(self, util, violation):
        return util if violation == 0 else -np.inf             # over the limit -> worst possible score

class StaticPenalty(ConstraintHandler):
    name = "Static penalty"
    def __init__(self, inst):
        super().__init__(inst)
        # fine per unit of overflow = highest utility any model earns per unit of any resource
        ratios = inst.p[None, :] / np.where(inst.R > 0, inst.R, np.nan)
        self.lam = np.nanmax(ratios)
    def fitness(self, util, violation):
        return util - self.lam * violation                     # utility minus the fine

class GreedyRepair(ConstraintHandler):
    def __init__(self, inst, weights, name):
        super().__init__(inst)
        self.name = name
        w = weights + 1e-6 * weights.max() * inst.b.mean() / inst.b      # tiny weight on every resource (tie-break)
        self.ratio = inst.p / (w @ inst.R)                               # value-for-money ratio u_j of each model
        self.drop_order = np.argsort(self.ratio, kind="stable")          # worst value first (used by DROP)
        self.add_order = self.drop_order[::-1].copy()                    # best value first (used by ADD)
        self.RT = np.ascontiguousarray(inst.R.T)                         # row j = resource use of model j (fast access)

    def initial(self, rng):
        return self.prepare(super().initial(rng))              # random selection, then repaired

    def prepare(self, x, keep=-1, ban=-1):
        x, RT, b = x.copy(), self.RT, self.I.b
        load = self.I.R @ x                                    # current use of each resource
        if (load > b).any():                                   # DROP: remove worst-value models until valid
            for j in self.drop_order:
                if x[j] and j != keep:                         # never remove the model the move just added
                    x[j] = 0
                    load -= RT[j]
                    if (load <= b).all():
                        break
        slack = b - load                                       # ADD: spare capacity of each resource
        # only models that are unselected and fit right now can ever be added (slack only shrinks)
        cand = self.add_order[(x[self.add_order] == 0) & (RT[self.add_order] <= slack).all(1)]
        for j in cand:                                         # best value first
            if j != ban and (RT[j] <= slack).all():            # never re-add the model the move just removed
                x[j] = 1
                slack -= RT[j]
        return x

    def fitness(self, util, violation):
        return util if violation == 0 else -np.inf             # never -inf in practice: repair output is always valid

# Repair with shadow-price weights (used throughout), and the simpler alternative compared in §4.1
def dual_repair(I):   return GreedyRepair(I, I.duals, "Repair (shadow-price weights)")
def naive_repair(I):  return GreedyRepair(I, 1.0 / I.b, "Repair (capacity-normalised weights)")

1.2 Variation operators¶

In [7]:
def neighbour(x, rng, p_swap=0.5):
    # Hill-climbing move. Returns (new selection, keep, ban) so the repair can preserve the move.
    #   flip: switch one random model in or out
    #   swap: remove one selected model and add one unselected model (same number of models)
    y, ones = x.copy(), np.flatnonzero(x)
    if rng.random() < p_swap and 0 < ones.size < x.size:      # swap needs at least one model in and one out
        i, j = rng.choice(ones), rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(x == 0))
        y[i], y[j] = 0, 1
        return y, j, i                                         # keep j (just added), ban i (just removed)
    j = rng.integers(x.size)
    y[j] ^= 1                                                  # flip model j
    return (y, j, -1) if y[j] else (y, -1, j)                  # added -> keep it; removed -> do not re-add it

def tournament(fit, rng, k=2):
    # Pick k random population members and return the index of the fittest one
    idx = rng.integers(fit.size, size=k)
    return idx[np.argmax(fit[idx])]

def uniform_crossover(a, b, rng):
    # For each model, copy the in/out decision from a random parent (50/50)
    return np.where(rng.random(a.size) < 0.5, a, b)

def bit_flip(x, pm, rng):
    # Flip each model's in/out decision independently with probability pm
    return x ^ (rng.random(x.size) < pm).astype(np.int8)

1.3 Algorithms¶

hill_climber (Part 1) and steady_state_ga (Part 2) work with any constraint handler. Their design choices and the reasons for them are given in P1.1 and P2.2. The GA also records population diversity (the average fraction of models on which two members disagree) every μ evaluations.

In [8]:
def hill_climber(I, handler, budget, rng, stall=300, p_swap=0.5):
    ev = Evaluator(I, budget)

    def start():
        # new starting selection and its fitness (costs one evaluation)
        x = handler.initial(rng)
        return x, handler.fitness(*ev.evaluate(x))

    cur, f_cur = start()
    since, restarts = 0, 0                      # evaluations since the last improvement, number of restarts
    while ev.remaining:
        y, keep, ban = neighbour(cur, rng, p_swap)          # propose a small change
        y = handler.prepare(y, keep, ban)                   # e.g. repair it (no-op for the penalty handlers)
        f_y = handler.fitness(*ev.evaluate(y))
        since = 0 if f_y > f_cur else since + 1             # count non-improving evaluations
        if f_y >= f_cur:                                    # accept if not worse (sideways moves allowed)
            cur, f_cur = y, f_y
        if since >= stall and ev.remaining:                 # stuck for too long -> random restart
            cur, f_cur = start()
            since, restarts = 0, restarts + 1
    return {**ev.result(), "restarts": restarts}, ev

def steady_state_ga(I, handler, budget, rng, pop_size=100, pm=None, k=2):
    ev, n = Evaluator(I, budget), I.n
    pm = 1.0 / n if pm is None else pm                      # default: about one bit flip per child
    pop, fit, seen = [], [], set()                          # `seen` holds every current member (as bytes)

    # 1) initial population of distinct selections (duplicates are skipped before evaluation)
    while len(pop) < pop_size and ev.remaining:
        x = handler.initial(rng)
        if x.tobytes() in seen:
            continue
        seen.add(x.tobytes()); pop.append(x); fit.append(handler.fitness(*ev.evaluate(x)))
    pop, fit = np.array(pop), np.array(fit)

    # 2) main loop: one child per step
    diversity, dup, streak = [], 0, 0
    while ev.remaining and streak < 10_000:                 # safety stop if only duplicates are produced
        c = uniform_crossover(pop[tournament(fit, rng, k)], pop[tournament(fit, rng, k)], rng)
        c = handler.prepare(bit_flip(c, pm, rng))           # mutate, then repair (if the handler repairs)
        key = c.tobytes()
        if key in seen:                                     # already in the population: discard, no evaluation
            dup += 1; streak += 1
            continue
        streak = 0
        f = handler.fitness(*ev.evaluate(c))
        w = np.argmin(fit)                                  # current worst member
        if f >= fit[w]:                                     # child replaces the worst if at least as good
            seen.discard(pop[w].tobytes()); seen.add(key)
            pop[w], fit[w] = c, f
        if ev.used % pop_size == 0:
            # diversity = average fraction of models on which two random members disagree
            q = pop.mean(0)
            diversity.append(2 * (q * (1 - q)).sum() / n * pop_size / (pop_size - 1))
    return {**ev.result(), "duplicates_skipped": dup}, ev, np.array(diversity)
In [9]:
def run_many(algo, I, make_handler, budget, n_runs=N_RUNS, label=None, **kw):
    # Run an algorithm n_runs times. Run k uses its own generator np.random.default_rng(MASTER_SEED + k).
    rows, traces, extras = [], [], []
    for k in range(n_runs):
        rng = np.random.default_rng(MASTER_SEED + k)
        handler = make_handler(I)
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        out = algo(I, handler, budget, rng, **kw)
        elapsed = time.perf_counter() - t0
        res, ev = out[0], out[1]
        # independent check: the reported best selection really respects every limit
        assert ev.best_x is not None and (I.R @ ev.best_x <= I.b).all()
        rows.append({"variant": label or handler.name, "run": k, **res, "time_s": elapsed})
        traces.append(ev.trace.copy())
        extras.append(out[2] if len(out) > 2 else None)    # e.g. GA diversity log
    return pd.DataFrame(rows), np.array(traces), extras

def summarise(df):
    # One row per variant: quality, reliability, validity rate and speed
    g = df.groupby("variant", sort=False)
    out = pd.DataFrame({
        "mean": g.best_utility.mean(), "std": g.best_utility.std(), "median": g.best_utility.median(),
        "best": g.best_utility.max(), "worst": g.best_utility.min(),
        "mean gap %": g["gap_%"].mean(), "success %": 100 * g.hit_optimum.mean(),
        "median evals→opt": g.evals_to_opt.median(), "feasible cand. %": 100 * g.feasible_rate.mean(),
        "time/run (s)": g.time_s.mean(), "µs / eval": 1e6 * g.time_s.sum() / g.evals_used.sum(),
    })
    if "duplicates_skipped" in df:                    # GA only: children discarded before evaluation
        out["dup. skipped / run"] = g.duplicates_skipped.mean()
    return out

def a12(a, b):
    # Vargha-Delaney A12: probability that a random run of A beats a random run of B (ties count half).
    # 0.5 = no difference, 1.0 = A always better, 0.0 = B always better.
    a, b = np.asarray(a, float)[:, None], np.asarray(b, float)[None, :]
    return (a > b).mean() + 0.5 * (a == b).mean()

def a12_magnitude(A):
    # standard Vargha-Delaney size labels
    d = abs(A - 0.5)
    return "negligible" if d < 0.06 else "small" if d < 0.14 else "medium" if d < 0.21 else "large"

def compare(a, b, alternative):
    # Mann-Whitney U test + A12 effect size. alternative: "greater", "less" or "two-sided".
    a, b = np.asarray(a, float), np.asarray(b, float)
    if np.unique(np.concatenate([a, b])).size == 1:
        U, p = a.size * b.size / 2, 1.0                    # all values identical: no evidence of any difference
    else:
        U, p = mannwhitneyu(a, b, alternative=alternative)
    A = a12(a, b)
    return {"median A": np.median(a), "median B": np.median(b), "U": U, "p": p,
            "A12": A, "effect": a12_magnitude(A)}

def holm(pvals):
    # Holm-Bonferroni correction: adjusts p-values when several tests are run on the same data
    p = np.asarray(pvals); order = np.argsort(p); adj = np.empty_like(p, dtype=float)
    running = 0
    for rank, i in enumerate(order):                        # smallest p first, multiplied by (tests left)
        running = max(running, (len(p) - rank) * p[i]); adj[i] = min(1.0, running)
    return adj
In [10]:
def plot_convergence(ax, traces, colors, optimum, title, logx=True, ylim=None):
    # One line per variant: median best-so-far utility over the runs, with a shaded band
    # from the 25th to the 75th percentile (the middle half of the runs)
    for (name, T), col in zip(traces.items(), colors):
        x = np.arange(1, T.shape[1] + 1)
        q1, med, q3 = np.percentile(T, [25, 50, 75], axis=0)
        ax.fill_between(x, q1, q3, color=col, alpha=0.18, linewidth=0)
        ax.plot(x, med, color=col, label=f"{name} (median, IQR band)")
    ax.axhline(optimum, color=C["muted"], ls="--", lw=1)            # dashed line = true optimum
    ax.annotate(f"optimum {optimum:,.0f}", (1, optimum), xycoords=("axes fraction", "data"),
                ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=8, color=C["muted"])
    if logx: ax.set_xscale("log")
    if ylim: ax.set_ylim(*ylim)
    ax.set(xlabel="fitness evaluations" + (" (log scale)" if logx else ""),
           ylabel="best feasible utility so far", title=title)
    ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=8)

def plot_box(ax, data, colors, title, ylabel="best utility at end of budget", optimum=None):
    # Boxplot per variant (line = median, diamond = mean), with every individual run shown as a dot
    names = list(data)
    bp = ax.boxplot([data[k] for k in names], widths=0.5, patch_artist=True,
                    medianprops=dict(color=C["ink"], lw=1.5), showmeans=True,
                    meanprops=dict(marker="D", markerfacecolor="white", markeredgecolor=C["ink"], markersize=6))
    for patch, col in zip(bp["boxes"], colors):
        patch.set(facecolor=col, alpha=0.55, edgecolor=col)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)                                   # small horizontal jitter so dots do not overlap
    for i, (k, col) in enumerate(zip(names, colors), start=1):
        ax.scatter(i + rng.uniform(-0.12, 0.12, len(data[k])), data[k], s=10, color=col, zorder=3, alpha=0.8)
    if optimum is not None:
        ax.axhline(optimum, color=C["muted"], ls="--", lw=1)
    ax.set_xticks(range(1, len(names) + 1), [k.replace(" (", "\n(") for k in names], fontsize=8)
    ax.set(title=title, ylabel=ylabel)

1.4 Correctness checks¶

The results only mean something if the building blocks are correct, so these checks run before any experiment:

  1. The repair output is always valid and full (10,000 random selections per instance, for both weightings).
  2. The Evaluator refuses to go over its budget.
  3. The exact solver is checked against brute force (trying all 2²⁰ ≈ 1 million selections) on a 20-model test problem.
  4. Our shadow prices (§0.2) are checked against the values from SciPy's LP solver. This is a check only; the algorithms use our own values.
In [11]:
# 1. Repair: random selections of random density must come out valid and full
rng = np.random.default_rng(MASTER_SEED)
for I in (I1, I2):
    for H in (dual_repair(I), naive_repair(I)):
        for _ in range(10_000):
            x = H.prepare((rng.random(I.n) < rng.random()).astype(np.int8))
            load = I.R @ x
            assert (load <= I.b).all()                                            # valid: no limit exceeded
            assert not ((I.R[:, x == 0] <= (I.b - load)[:, None]).all(0)).any()   # full: no unselected model fits
print("1. repair: 40,000 random vectors -> all feasible and maximal")

# 2. Evaluator: a 4th evaluation on a budget of 3 must be refused
ev = Evaluator(I1, 3); [ev.evaluate(np.zeros(I1.n, np.int8)) for _ in range(3)]
try:
    ev.evaluate(np.zeros(I1.n, np.int8)); raise RuntimeError("budget not enforced")
except AssertionError:
    print("2. evaluator: budget strictly enforced")

# 3. Exact solver vs brute force on the first 20 models of Instance 1 (tighter capacities)
sub = slice(0, 20); p, R, b = I1.p[sub], I1.R[:, sub], I1.b * 0.6
X = ((np.arange(2**20)[:, None] >> np.arange(20)) & 1).astype(np.int8)     # every 0/1 combination
brute = (X @ p)[((X @ R.T) <= b).all(1)].max()                              # best valid one
exact = -milp(-p, constraints=LinearConstraint(R, -np.inf, b), integrality=np.ones(20), bounds=Bounds(0, 1)).fun
print(f"3. exhaustive search = {brute:,.0f}, MILP = {exact:,.0f} -> {'match' if brute == exact else 'MISMATCH'}")
del X

# 4. Our shadow prices vs SciPy's LP solver (validation only: not used by any algorithm)
from scipy.optimize import linprog
for I in (I1, I2):
    lp = linprog(-I.p, A_ub=I.R, b_ub=I.b, bounds=(0, 1), method="highs")
    diff = np.abs(I.duals - (-lp.ineqlin.marginals)).max()
    print(f"4. {I.name}: own shadow prices vs SciPy LP duals, max |difference| = {diff:.1e}; "
          f"bound {I.bound:,.2f} vs {-lp.fun:,.2f} -> {'match' if diff < 1e-2 else 'MISMATCH'}")

2. evaluator: budget strictly enforced

Part 1: Baseline discrete local search (Instance 1, n = 28, m = 2)¶

P1.1 Design choices¶

Element Choice Reason
Representation 0/1 vector x ∈ {0,1}²⁸ matches the decision variables directly, and every operator keeps it a valid 0/1 vector
Starting point random bits (each model in with probability 0.5), then the handler's own start rule unbiased start; each handler decides how to make it valid
Move (mutation) flip (prob. 0.5) or swap 1-out/1-in (prob. 0.5) A good selection is nearly full on both resources (the optimum uses 495/500 and 499/500). From there, adding a model breaks a limit and removing one loses utility, so a flip-only climber gets stuck quickly. A swap exchanges models at roughly the same resource use, which is the move that can still improve a full selection
Acceptance accept the first neighbour that is at least as good one neighbour per evaluation (cheap); sideways moves let it cross flat regions
Escape random restart after 300 evaluations without improvement otherwise the climber stays stuck at the first local optimum
Budget 3,000 evaluations per run, M = 30 runs the same for all three strategies

Constraint-strategy test. The brief describes Instance 1 as the instance for constraint strategy testing. So the same climber is run with each of the three handlers from §1.1 (death penalty, static penalty, shadow-price repair). Only the constraint handling differs, so its effect is isolated, and the result justifies which strategy the rest of the notebook uses.

P1.2 Discussion¶

  • Constraint handling matters more than the search moves. With the same moves, acceptance rule and budget, the repair-based climber finds the true optimum (130,883) in all 30 runs, usually within a few dozen evaluations. The death-penalty and static-penalty climbers never reach it, and their results vary widely between runs (see table and boxplot). Both differences are significant (Mann–Whitney p ≪ 0.001, A12 = 1.0).
  • Why the penalty climbers fail. About half of their moves produce an over-limit selection, which is either rejected outright (death penalty) or heavily fined (static penalty), see "feasible cand. %". Near the limits, the only moves left are removing a model or swapping two models with very similar resource use, so these climbers get stuck often. Restarts help, but 3,000 evaluations are not enough.
  • Why repair works. Every repaired selection is valid and full: the ADD step fills any spare capacity with the best-value models, so each evaluation tests a complete, sensible selection. A flip effectively becomes "force model j in, then rebuild the rest", a much bigger and better-informed step. The keep/ban rule makes sure this step never just returns the current selection.
  • Cost. Repair costs extra computing time per evaluation (≈ 2.5× more µs/eval, see table). On this instance that does not matter, since a whole run takes well under a second.

Decision: repair is used as the constraint-handling strategy for Part 2. Part 3 tests whether its advantage over a penalty also holds on the larger instance, and at what cost.

Part 2: Advanced metaheuristic (Instance 2, n = 90, m = 5)¶

P2.1 Algorithm choice: steady-state GA with greedy repair (after Chu & Beasley, 1998)¶

The Chu–Beasley GA is a well-known population method for the 0-1 multidimensional knapsack problem, tested on the standard OR-Library benchmarks for this problem type. I reimplemented its core ideas from scratch, with three engineering changes:

  • one repair interface for both algorithms: the same repair code serves the hill climber (Part 1) and the GA;
  • duplicate children are rejected before evaluation, using a hash set, so no budget is wasted on selections already in the population;
  • a budgeted evaluator, so every comparison uses exactly the same number of evaluations.

P2.2 Why these operators¶

Component Choice Why (and why not the alternatives)
Population model steady-state, μ = 100, child replaces the worst member if at least as good A new child joins the population immediately and can be a parent in the very next step, so good children are used faster than in a generational GA. Only the worst member is ever replaced, so the best selection is never lost (elitism without extra code)
Selection binary tournament mild, constant selection pressure (keeps diversity) and cheap. It only compares which of two is better, so it does not depend on the size of the fitness values. Roulette-wheel selection would be nearly random here, because all utilities are around 11,000 and differ only slightly
Crossover uniform The order of the models in the list means nothing, so there are no "neighbouring" models worth keeping together. One-point and two-point crossover would only add a bias towards inheriting models with nearby index numbers. Uniform crossover has no such bias (Syswerda, 1989): models both parents agree on are kept, and the rest is a fair 50/50 choice
Mutation bit-flip, pₘ = 1/n (about 1 flip per child) a small change to what the child inherited. The repair then rebalances it, so the actual change is larger, without destroying what was inherited
Constraint handling greedy DROP/ADD repair with shadow-price weights Part 1 showed repair clearly beats the penalty approaches. Every evaluated child is valid and full, so no evaluations are wasted on over-limit selections. The shadow prices (§0.2) say how scarce each resource is. Only resource 2 has a positive price, so the ratio $p_j / \lambda_2 r_{2j}$ ranks models by utility per unit of the resource that actually runs out
Diversity duplicate rejection stops the population filling up with copies of the best selection, a known problem when a GA repairs every child

Cost per child: crossover and mutation take time proportional to n, and repair and evaluation proportional to n·m. The ratio order is computed once per run.

P2.3 Discussion¶

  • Quality: the GA reaches the true optimum (11,191) in 30/30 runs, after a median of a few hundred evaluations. That is a tiny fraction (about 10⁻²⁴) of the 2⁹⁰ possible selections.
  • Validity: the audit table checks the best selection independently. Resource 2 is used to exactly 100 %, as the shadow prices predicted, and every other resource has spare capacity.
  • Diversity: starts high (random repaired selections), drops as selection takes effect, and levels off above zero. Duplicate rejection stops it from collapsing completely, so the GA keeps exploring after it has found the optimum.
  • Hidden cost of duplicate rejection. Repair turns many different children into the same full selection. Once the population has converged, most children are duplicates and are thrown away without using budget (dup. skipped / run). Each one still costs a crossover, a mutation and a repair, so computing time per evaluation grows after convergence. Part 3 measures this cost against a penalty-based GA.

Whether the population is actually needed on this instance, or whether the Part 1 hill climber would do just as well, is examined in §4.2.

Part 3: Empirical study and hypothesis testing (Instance 2)¶

P3.1 Research question and hypothesis¶

Part 1 showed that repair beats penalties on the small instance. Here we test whether that holds on the challenge instance inside the GA, and at what cost. The two variants differ only in how they handle constraints:

  • Variant A, repair: every child is repaired with the shadow-price repair (the Part 2 GA).
  • Variant B, static penalty: children are not repaired. Over-limit children get the fine from §1.1.

Hypothesis H1. The repair GA reaches a higher final utility than the penalty GA under the same evaluation budget.

Why we expect this. The optimum sits exactly on the limit of resource 2 (100 % used). A penalty GA can only reach that limit through selection: part of its budget goes on over-limit children that can never count as a solution, and uniform crossover of two parents near the limit often produces an over-limit child. Repair turns every child into a full, valid selection, so every evaluation is a usable candidate.

Possible counter-argument. The penalty GA is much cheaper per evaluation, because it skips the repair. With equal computing time rather than equal evaluations, it might catch up. §P3.4 tests this directly.

H0: both variants have the same distribution of final utility. H1 (one-sided): repair > penalty.

P3.2 Protocol¶

  • Equal budget: 5,000 fitness evaluations per run, counted by the shared Evaluator, so neither variant can evaluate more.
  • M = 30 independent runs per variant. Run k of each variant uses seed 42 + k. The two variants make different random choices from the first step onwards, so the two sets of runs are treated as independent samples.
  • Only the constraint handling changes. Everything else stays fixed: steady-state GA, μ = 100, binary tournament, uniform crossover, pₘ = 1/n, duplicate rejection.
  • Statistics: one-sided Mann–Whitney U test at α = 0.05. It is non-parametric, so it does not assume normally distributed results, which matters here because many runs end exactly at the optimum. It is reported with the Vargha–Delaney A12 effect size (the chance that a random run of one variant beats a random run of the other), as recommended for randomised algorithms by Arcuri & Briand (2011).

CPU cost per evaluation: repair 832 µs, penalty 109 µs  ->  ratio 7.6x

H1 is supported. With the same budget of 5,000 evaluations, the repair GA reaches the optimum in every run. The penalty GA never reaches it, and ends lower and with more spread. The difference is large and highly significant (A12 = 1.0). The right-hand panel shows why: about 41 % of the penalty GA's evaluations are spent on over-limit children, which can never count as a solution and only influence selection. Every repair evaluation is a valid, full selection.

P3.4 Equal computing time¶

Equal evaluation budgets are the standard way to compare fairly, but repair does extra work inside prepare() that the evaluation count does not show. To check whether H1 only holds because we count evaluations rather than time, the penalty GA is run again with a budget that gives it roughly the same total computing time as the repair GA. The budget is fixed at 37,500 evaluations (5,000 × 7.5), because the cost ratio measured on the development machine was 7.5× (the cell above prints the ratio on the current machine). A fixed number keeps the result reproducible.

Repair(5k) vs Penalty(37.5k): p=1.67e-01, A12=0.52 (negligible)

With equal computing time, H1 is not supported. Given 37,500 evaluations (about the same total time, see the time/run column), the penalty GA reaches the optimum in 29/30 runs, and the difference from repair is no longer significant (p ≈ 0.17, A12 ≈ 0.52, negligible).

P3.5 Discussion: quality, constraint enforcement and time¶

The advantage of repair is that it gets more out of each evaluation. If evaluations were expensive (for example, testing each model selection on real hardware), repair would clearly be the better choice. With a cheap objective like this one, a penalty GA given enough time gets there too.

Two details keep this conclusion fair to repair:

  • Most of the 7.5× extra time comes from duplicates, not from the repair itself. After it has found the optimum (median 340 evaluations), the repair GA keeps producing children that the repair turns back into existing population members, and about 16,000 are discarded per run (dup. skipped / run). In the Part 1 hill climber, which has no duplicate check, repair costs only ≈ 2.5× a plain evaluation. Stopping once the population has converged, or mutating duplicates more strongly, would remove most of this overhead.
  • Repair still reaches the optimum sooner in real time. Repair needs a median of 340 evaluations × at most 0.8 ms ≈ at most 0.3 s (an upper estimate, since most duplicates appear after convergence). The penalty GA needs ≈ 10,100 evaluations × 0.11 ms ≈ 1.1 s.
Repair (shadow prices) Static penalty
Solution quality optimum in 30/30 runs (5k evals) optimum in 0/30 runs at 5k evals, 29/30 at 37.5k (≈ equal time)
Constraint enforcement 100 % of evaluated candidates valid, guaranteed by the repair ~41 % (5k) to 53 % (37.5k) of evaluations over the limit. Final validity depends on choosing the fine λ well
Computing time per evaluation high: the repair itself, plus duplicates after convergence low (one matrix–vector product)
Problem knowledge needed a ranking of the models (shadow prices, §0.2) only the fine λ
What can go wrong a poor ranking slows it down (§4.1) λ too small → over-limit selections score best; λ too large → the search avoids the limit and misses the optimum

4. Additional experiments (beyond the brief)¶

The main results raise two follow-up questions, answered here with the same protocol (30 runs, equal budgets, Mann–Whitney U + A12):

  • §4.1 Which repair weights work best? The repair is the most problem-specific part of the design. Do the shadow prices actually matter, or would a simpler weighting do?
  • §4.2 Does the population help? The GA solved Instance 2 easily. Would the Part 1 hill climber have done just as well, and if so, when is the GA worth it?

4.1 Which repair weights work best?¶

The repair ranks models by value for money, utility ÷ weighted resource use, and the weights decide which resources count. We compare:

  • Shadow-price weights (used so far): $p_j/\sum_i \lambda_i r_{ij}$. Only scarce resources count; on Instance 2 that is resource 2 alone.
  • Capacity-normalised weights: $p_j/\sum_i r_{ij}/b_i$. Each resource counts as a fraction of its capacity, and all five count equally. This is the usual default, also used in the module's lab notebook.

Hypothesis H2. Shadow-price repair reaches the optimum in fewer evaluations than capacity-normalised repair.

Why we expect this. The capacity-normalised ratio also counts the four resources that are not scarce. A model that uses little of resource 2 but a lot of the others then looks expensive and is dropped first, even though removing it frees almost none of the resource that is actually short. The shadow-price ratio charges nothing for resources with spare capacity, so DROP removes the models with the least utility per unit of resource 2, and ADD fills resource 2 as profitably as possible.

What we measure. (i) The number of evaluations needed to reach the true optimum (a run that never reaches it is counted as budget + 1, which keeps it ranked last). (ii) The best utility reached after 100, 250, 500 and 1,000 evaluations, to see which variant is ahead early on. Because these five tests use the same runs, their p-values are Holm-corrected so the overall false-positive rate stays at 5 %.

In [20]:
# Why should the weights matter? Compare the two rankings, and each repair's greedy result on its own.
Hd, Hn = dual_repair(I2), naive_repair(I2)
rho = spearmanr(Hd.ratio, Hn.ratio).statistic        # 1.0 = identical ranking of the 90 models
g_d = I2.p @ Hd.prepare(np.zeros(I2.n, np.int8)); g_n = I2.p @ Hn.prepare(np.zeros(I2.n, np.int8))
print(f"Spearman rank correlation of the two pseudo-utility orderings: rho = {rho:.2f}")
print(f"Pure greedy (ADD from empty), no search: shadow-price = {g_d:,.0f} (gap {100*(I2.optimum-g_d)/I2.optimum:.2f} %), "
      f"normalised = {g_n:,.0f} (gap {100*(I2.optimum-g_n)/I2.optimum:.2f} %)")

# The shadow-price variant is the Part 2 GA (A_rep); only the capacity-normalised variant needs new runs
B_nai, B_nai_tr, _ = run_many(steady_state_ga, I2, naive_repair, P3_BUDGET, label="Repair (capacity-normalised weights)")
B_df = pd.concat([A_rep, B_nai], ignore_index=True)
summarise(B_df)

H2 is supported. Both repairs reach the optimum eventually, because the GA can make up for a weaker repair given enough evaluations. But the shadow-price repair gets there in significantly fewer evaluations: about half as many at the median, a large effect. After Holm correction it is also significantly ahead after 100, 250 and 500 evaluations. By 1,000 evaluations both have converged, and the difference is no longer significant.

Why it happens. The two rankings are similar but not identical (Spearman ρ ≈ 0.84), and the models they disagree on are exactly the ones that decide the optimum. The shadow-price greedy alone, with no search at all, already gets within 0.21 % of the optimum, while the normalised greedy is 3.3 % away. A better ranking gives a better starting population and a better repair of every child. (The normalised repair actually uses less computing time per evaluation, because it converges later and so produces fewer duplicates.)

Takeaway: the repair is where knowledge about the problem enters the GA, and shadow prices are a cheap, well-founded way to provide it. The difference shows in how fast the optimum is found rather than whether it is found, which is why evaluations-to-optimum is reported alongside final quality.

4.2 Does the population help?¶

Question. In Part 2 the GA solved Instance 2 in every run. Would the simpler Part 1 hill climber, given the same repair and the same 5,000 evaluations, have done just as well? And if so, is there a setting where the GA's population makes a real difference?

Approach. First, the hill climber with shadow-price repair is run on Instance 2 and compared with the Part 2 GA. Then both algorithms are tested in two harder settings that take away the help of a near-perfect repair order (30 runs, 3,000 evaluations each):

  • (a) Weaker repair: Instance 2 with the capacity-normalised repair, which §4.1 showed is the weaker ranking. The search has to correct a badly ranked repair.
  • (b) Harder instance: Instance 2 with all capacities multiplied by 0.3 (Instance 2-T). Its shadow prices show two scarce resources (R1 and R2), so no single ratio ranks the models perfectly. The exact optimum is again computed for scoring only.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4.2))

On the original instance, no. The hill climber also reaches the optimum in 30/30 runs, and there is no significant difference in how many evaluations each needs (two-sided test above). With only one scarce resource and a near-perfect repair order (§4.1: the shadow-price greedy alone gets within 0.21 % of the optimum), the repair does most of the work, and a good local search is enough.

In the harder settings, yes. The GA reaches the optimum far more reliably than the climber in both stress tests, a large and significant difference (see outputs):

  • (a) Weaker repair: the climber's one-at-a-time exchanges often get stuck at a local optimum, and its restarts end up in a similar place because the same badly ranked repair is applied again. The GA combines models that different population members got right, which fixes ranking errors that no single move can fix.
  • (b) Two scarce resources: improving a selection now often means exchanging several models at once to keep both resources within limits. Uniform crossover followed by repair makes such multi-model changes naturally, while the climber changes only one or two models at a time.

Takeaway: the GA is the more robust choice. On the original instance its advantage is hidden by a very good repair, but it shows as soon as the problem or the repair gets harder.

5. Conclusions and limitations¶

  1. Part 1: on Instance 1, the constraint handling decided the outcome. With the same moves and budget, a move-preserving greedy repair turned a weak hill climber (penalty versions: optimum never found) into one that finds the true optimum in 30/30 runs.
  2. Part 2: a steady-state GA built from scratch, with shadow-price repair (prices computed by our own Lagrangian routine), uniform crossover and duplicate rejection, finds the true optimum of Instance 2 in 30/30 runs.
  3. Part 3: H1 is supported with equal evaluation budgets (A12 = 1.0), but not with roughly equal computing time, where a well-chosen static penalty catches up (29/30 optimal). The repair GA still reaches the optimum about 4× sooner in real time, and most of its extra cost comes from avoidable duplicates.
  4. Additional experiments: shadow-price weights make the repair about twice as efficient as capacity-normalised weights (H2, large effect, Holm-corrected). The GA and the hill climber perform equally on the original instance, but in the two harder stress-test settings the GA reaches the optimum in every run while the climber manages only 30–40 %.

Limitations.

  • Generalisation: there is only one challenge instance, and it has a single scarce resource. On instances where several resources are scarce, the shadow prices spread across resources and the H2 advantage should shrink. Testing that would need more instances with tighter constraints (e.g. the OR-Library mknapcb set).
  • What the evaluation count measures: it ignores the cost of repair, which is why §P3.4 adds a computing-time check. Absolute times depend on the machine; the relative ranking is what matters.
  • Settings: the penalty weight λ was chosen by a rule rather than tuned. An adaptive penalty (Hadj-Alouane & Bean, 1997) was tried during development but never kicked in, because the best member stayed valid. Uniform crossover, pₘ = 1/n and μ = 100 were not tuned separately for each variant. Both variants share them, so the comparison is fair, but other settings could change the effect sizes.
  • Statistics: 30 runs per variant, non-parametric tests, effect sizes, and Holm correction where several tests share the same runs.
